utterances.text: No, Your Honour. He says, Is it not true that one of these men said that Milan Lukic visited. If he asked that second question, I wouldn't have an objection, but he started off by saying, I have information for one of these men, and then he asks: "Do you deny that this is not true?" That's specifically asking for him to comment on what this other individual, undeclared, unknown, is telling Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, it is not a fact that while you were detained in a Visegrad police station, Milan Lukic, a reserve police officer - albeit against his will, allegedly - was in that police station every night that you were, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: No, no, it's not true, and it's not true that this other guy that you mentioned a bit earlier. He didn't come. I mean, there is talk that he did come. That's what is circulating around. But actually, neither he nor the other guy came around, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify whether what is not true, Mr. Groome, is that Milan Lukic did not visit him every night or whether he came once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever see Milan Lukic during the time that you were under arrest in the Visegrad police station come into the police station, at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I only saw this first guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that we are clear about the time-period, this is in May of 1992, correct, the time that you were detained in the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, what have you been doing for employment the last few years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Nothing. I mean, I have my own small truck and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would you characterise -- are you steadily busy working with that truck or has it been difficult to earn a living in these times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: It is difficult to work. There isn't work constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was this an apartment that both of you took under lease in preparation for becoming married?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: No. No, this was the apartment that her boss was paying for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did she live there alone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Yes. My father knew, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And at this point in time, were you already a member of the Federation army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You at some point did join the Federation army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: At some point, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: This was in July, early July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about this apartment. How many floors were in the building that this apartment was in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: There were five or six families there, perhaps three or four families. There was a room rented there for that employee who worked close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how many floors in the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: The ground floor and two floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you be shown a picture of this neighbourhood. I ask that it not be displayed to the public. It is ERN 0544-9983.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, in a short while, the photograph will come up before you. I'm going to ask you with the assistance of the court usher to take an electronic pen and circle the apartment where you were with your girlfriend.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: This is the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you mentioned another building that you -- or an abandoned house that you stayed in for several days. Can you tell us the name of the person who owned that house without compromising your identity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I can. Shall I tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Nedjic Sabanovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please circle the abandoned building where you stayed for that period of days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, did you know a woman by the name of Behija Zukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I cannot remember. It sounds familiar, but I can't remember the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They appear to be a well known family that had a grocery store in town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I heard of that. They are well known, but it was a long time ago. It's the faces, the faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. I'm finished with that. I at this time, Your Honour, would tender that photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P228 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, were you present in the apartment of your girlfriend the day that Murat Sabanovic released water from the dam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know where you were that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I do know. I was there in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that we go into closed session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that your girlfriend was a waitress in the bar in the area in which she lived. Were you a regular patron of that bar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Yes, mostly. Although I would go more to see her in the apartment than to the restaurant. You know, she was a waitress so the guests would be, you know, commenting and saying things. You know how it is if you are a waitress. So I avoided going to her place of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've told us here this morning that she was your fiancee, that you proposed marriage to her during this five to six months that you were seeing her. Your statement says absolutely nothing about being engaged to her, simply refers to her as a friend from the bar. Why did you forget to include that in your statement? It seems like an important fact.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I was just rolling back in my mind all the events, all the things I could remember, and I remembered immediately. Well, the first half we were like that. I mean, it wasn't that we were ready for marriage. We were just courting, and it was like this, and then towards the end we had agreed to get married, and it was a custom to buy, like, a gold chain or a ring or something like that as an engagement gift.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, please tell us the day that you got engaged and gave your girlfriend a piece of jewellery.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Maybe a month before the 4th, before we went where we went.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, I was asking for the date. You do remember the date that you were engaged with your girlfriend, no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember. It was about a month before, and then after that, the trip and the meeting with this one, so a month prior. That would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, well, what day did you plan on getting married? Had you set a date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Not properly. No, we didn't set a proper date. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's okay. Let him answer this one. Too late for the objection, Your Honours, but if -- Mr. Groome should perhaps ask about the customs that are in place in Bosnia, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll leave that for redirect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, how is it you remember the 4th of June with such precision that police arrived at your door but seem to be having difficulty recalling the date that you were engaged to the love of your life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: It's hard for me to remember. I know it was a month before that, but she was really screaming. I mean, she was afraid, you understand, and then she said, We will not forget this ever, if we do manage to get out, if we get out in two or three days. You understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I do understand that. This is the third time now you've been taken into custody against your will. You are not able to tell me the date that you were placed on the back of your truck with your father; is that correct? You cannot give me the precise date there, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: The exact date, the 12th, the 13th. I cannot know exactly the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: But I think I cannot recall these meetings with this -- my ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The record records you as saying: "But I think I cannot recall these meetings with this -- my..." and then it seems that you did not finish your answer. Could I ask you to please complete your answer? What meetings can you not recall?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can intervene, and again, this is a an issue for the transcript, if I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm aware that there may be some issues with the transcript, but I'm growing increasingly concerned that this is being -- translation corrections are being used to coach witnesses in the middle of their testimony. I'd ask that if there's a translation issue that it be handled in the appropriate way. If Mr. Ivetic tells me that my question has been mistranslated, I will certainly repeat my question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. No, the basis for Mr. Groome's question has been mistranslated, Your Honours, and if I'm not to correct it, then let's proceed like this, let's -- but I think you should ask the -- well, the audio will prove me correct. Let it just stand at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, again, the transcript records you as saying you cannot recall these meetings. Did you say that, and if you said that, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Which meetings? You were asking a lot. Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll go back to my original question. You are not able to recall the precise date that you and your father were forcibly placed on a truck and brought to the stadium; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: 12th or the 13th, something like that. That's how I remember the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the day, the precise date that you were arrested and brought to the Visegrad police station for two or three days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Precise date. About 15 days after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your reference point is that it's about two weeks after the initial time that you were arrested, the day the Uzice Corps came into town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: The Uzice Corps, I think on or about the 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The 1st of what month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, your girlfriend or former fiancee is deceased now; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What's the date of her death?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know. I asked, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was going to say, that flows from his testimony before as to how he learned of the circumstances of the death and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there an objection to the question I've asked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He's already asked this once, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just carry on, please. Carry on. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, earlier today you said that -- at transcript 12, line 11, you said that the police arrived at your house on the 4th of June sometime in the morning. Looking at paragraph 3 of the statement that we were provided by Defence, it says that it was in the afternoon. So I ask you, was it in the morning or was it in the afternoon that the police first came to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: To that neighbourhood at my girlfriend's place, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: About noon, morning, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your statement is wrong when it records you as saying it was in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I don't know that. I know that that same date before that, we went to that abandoned house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, it's your testimony that you never saw Milan Lukic before this day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it's your testimony that after he dropped you off in Novi Pazar, you had never seen him again during the course of the war or after the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I see him since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I notice when you walked into the courtroom, you actually greeted someone. Was the person that you greeted and waved back to you, is that the person that you're describing as Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look around the courtroom, and just so it's clear who we are speaking about, can you indicate where the person you are referring to as Milan Lukic is sitting in the courtroom, perhaps by the row that they're sitting in and their position from left to right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Right next to the policeman on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the tie that he is wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: It's got some grey. It's got some white.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, sir, I notice that you waved to him within taking a couple of steps after walking in this courtroom. Am I right to conclude from that that you recognised him almost immediately after walking into this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Well, I recognised him on TV, as well, even before I walked into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does he appear to be different to you in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: A little. A little different. A little older, plumper.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, on paragraph 4 of your statement, it says: "When the third light-brown-haired, tall, and big policeman saw that, he asked his fellow colleagues not to take us in, since there was nothing disputable about our documents." Do you describe his hair colour from that period as being light brown?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does it appear darker to you as he sits here today, or is that the colour that you recall from 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: A little darker.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in this very first encounter with you, you describe that he tells you a number of things about his life: where he has been, how he is forced against his will to be a police officer, and that his mother was sick. How long did this go on, this kind of sharing of some of the important events in his life on this first occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: A short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did he volunteer this information about his mother and where he was before Visegrad and what happened with the police? Did he volunteer this to you, or was this in response to questions you asked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: He told us what he said, against his will, back from Switzerland, in order to take his mother there because his mother was ill or something, and that was when we realised that one could actually talk to him. And then we asked him, Come on, give us a hand with this certificate business so they -- and all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, it's been put to some witnesses at this trial that there were a lot of rumours flying around about Milan Lukic, that a lot of people were talking about things that he was supposed to have done. Had you heard any rumours about crimes or violent acts that a person by the name of Milan Lukic had been perpetrating?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll object as to foundation without a period of time being identified, and it's -- from 1992 to present is a long time. If it could be broken down, I think the witness ought to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Unless I say differently, I'm talking about the day that we're talking about now in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you remember my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Can you repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Around this time, the time that you first meet Milan Lukic, it's been put to witnesses that there were many, many wild rumours flying around about terribly violent acts that he was perpetrating. Had you yourself heard any of these rumours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: No. I heard more after the war when everything was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's also been put to witnesses that there were rumours that he was in possession of a red Passat that was taken from a prominent Muslim woman who was killed. Did you hear any of these rumours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll let the answer stand, but, I mean, it's re-asking the same question. He said he heard no bad rumours. Then the counsel puts to him, Did you hear the rumour that he did this? It's asked and answered, but the question -- the witness answered in the negative so it stands. But I think that such questions are irrelevant without bases after they received the original answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to read a portion of your statement. In paragraph 4, it says: "I asked him to take us to Serbia where I would make a plan where to hide because I was in fear because of warfare in the territory of Visegrad." Is it your testimony that within minutes of meeting this Serb police officer, you asked him to help you escape from Visegrad? A simple yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: He had introduced himself and told us he, too, was a --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What were you yourself trying to escape in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Well, many things. There was firing. You weren't safe. It applied to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what it not be fair to say that given your experience in the Visegrad police station, that you believed that police officers were among the people that were committing violent acts against some of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I don't get this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you spent two to three days in the Visegrad police station. While you were there, did you not witness some of the violent acts perpetrated by members of that police force against some of the Muslims detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: No. The soldiers, it was the soldiers who were beating us, soldiers, members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that soldiers came into the police station and mistreated the people detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was it about Milan Lukic that made you entrust your very life to him so quickly and so completely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Because he was open to us as well. He told us what he told us, and my judgement was that he might be trusted in terms of getting us out. It wasn't until later that I found out when he talked to my girlfriend during the trip itself and he was asking her, Do you remember this, Do you remember that. I think he was even a customer where she worked, at that cafe, and I felt then at the time that she, too, had remembered him from before. So this whole story --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, if you feel that you can trust him with the life of you and your fiancee, why not ask him to also save your father and your brother? Why not also ask him to save the remainder of your family, help all of you get out of Visegrad at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Well, that was the first time I set eyes on him. The army and all that, that was before, and I reckoned I would try and get my father out of there once I'd put up my girlfriend, and my girlfriend and a colleague confirmed that there was an avenue for them to be pulled out. That was why I travelled all the way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, at this time, you did not know anyone in Belgrade; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the answer. The interpreter didn't understand anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you just to lean a little bit closer to the microphone and repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I don't know Belgrade that much, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why is it that you ask him to take you there instead of to the other side of Visegrad where you could have safely made your way to Gorazde or some of the other areas held by Bosnian Federation forces? Why to a place full of Serbs that you don't know anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Because it was something that he could do while he was busy with another task. It was about the certificates and him being able to take his mother there, but you see, the Muslim forces and once they get going, you know, it's not a great distance, and then you have to pound all those Serb obstacles and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You only state in your statement about one check-point that you encountered on your way to Belgrade. Is it true that you only went through one check-point?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: At Uvac, that check-point, is that the one you mean, with a small bridge, the one that we walked across?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is the only one that you mentioned. Am I correct in thinking that that particular check-point, Uvac, is still within the municipality of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: It's straddles the border with Serbia, over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was it the border crossing with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You encountered no other check-points on the way out of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Nothing much, really. Those check-points, they didn't ask for no papers, but here, yes, they did. We knew exactly how far we could go without this stamp, certificate, whatever you called that, because it was that one that we needed it for, the one at Uvac, right, because we walked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, at this time you did not have a passport, so you are crossing an international check-point, a border crossing check-point without a passport; is that correct? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, misstates the evidence. The witness was very clear as to how and where he crossed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's asking him whether that's his evidence. That's for him to say. Is that what you are saying, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one asked to see the passport, just the ID and all that, and the certificates, which -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, Mr. Ivetic took 51 minutes, and you have now used an hour and 15 minutes. How much more do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd say about another 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want to finish this witness today, so I'll give you another 12 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that shortly after you were in Novi Pazar you came back to Visegrad on a public transportation; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did you show at the border crossing when you returned into Visegrad or into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I had my ID on me. Entering Bosnia, that bus, no one asked for anything. It's not a problem getting into Bosnia or Visegrad specifically. The problem is getting out. Getting out. On your way into Visegrad, you don't need a certificate or anything, but if you want to leave Visegrad, no way. There are check-points where you have to produce this certificate, that certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that Map 0545-2690 be placed on the screen for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm asking that a map be placed before you. Can I ask you what you recall about Milan Lukic's apartment. How many floors were in the apartment building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Three or four. Three or four floors. We were in one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: And I know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the apartment have property belonging to Milan Lukic in it, property such as a telephone, a television, different types of property you would normally find in an apartment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: It was a furnished flat, yes, furnished with that counter, the bed that I told you about, with leather --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's no need to re-describe it again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: -- that we were in, and then the other side, the terrace and all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to take a look at -- there's a map of Belgrade before you. Would you be able to circle the approximate area of where you were in Belgrade during this period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I can't find my way around this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you are not able, sir, I don't want to waste any time on it. If you're able to quickly circle the approximate location of where you were ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I remember it was called Bezanijska Kosa, something like that, but I'm looking at this and I'm wondering, what's all of this about? You get it, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you're not able, sir, then I'll move on. Sir, are you able to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you, court usher. Sir, you arrived there on the 7th and you went to Novi Pazar on the 10th; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, looking at the statement that you've given, both translations, the ones we were provided and the ones that is purported to be of CLSS, all of those statements say that you stayed there either four days or four nights. By my calculations, the 7th to the 10th would simply be the three; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I'm doing the math myself, the 4th, the 5th, the 6th, the 7th. So those were the three days. The 7th, the 8th, the 9th and the 10th. That was my calculation, four days, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, the CLSS translation that we were just provided says that you spent four nights in the apartment. If you stayed there the night of the 7th, you stayed there the night of the 8th, the night of the 9th, that would be three nights, and then if you went to Pazar on the 10th, that would be three nights in the apartment; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we can have the -- Mr. Groome, if he's going to refer to the statement, the witness's language is Bosnian. He signed a Bosnian statement. Have him refer to the Bosnian statement that the counsel has actually introduced into evidence, and we can -- in these translations --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, given my limited time, I'd rather not have Mr. Ivetic read a statement. Let him use his redirect for that. I'll move on to another area. The witness has testified and he has counted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, but Mr. Groome, if you are putting a statement to him, then I agree, it should be put in --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That language he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- the language that he knows, and I'll take that into account. Can we have it in the language that he -- in his language.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's being brought up, may I ask a few more questions, and then we'll come back to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can assist, it's page 2 in the middle -- page 2 of the B/C/S. In the middle is the selection that Mr. Groome was citing to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, while the court officer is pulling up this portion of your statement, when did you decide with your girlfriend that you would go to Novi Pazar? At what point in the three or four days was the decision taken that you would try to make your way to Novi Pazar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I decided that when we were staying in that flat. We were discussing all sorts of things, who and where, who knows whom and where, and then she said this about this colleague in Novi Pazar, best thing to do, just go there to visit her.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can draw your attention to the morning of the 8th, are you able to tell me whether you came to the decision to go to Novi Pazar before the morning of the 8th of June or after the morning of the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: After, towards the end was when we -- because we were thinking and thinking, and it was in the last day that we eventually decided to go there because we didn't know of any better option.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So are you saying that it was not until the 10th of June that you made a decision with your girlfriend that your best option was to go to Novi Pazar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Well, we were taking our time to decide, but the decision was taken towards the end. But it was something that we were doing throughout the time we spent there, what would be the best thing for us to do, where to go, where's the safest place to go, does anyone know anyone else anywhere, that sort of thing, and then we took the decision, and when it was final, because she had this friend over there in this town, well, best place to go, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The record records you at page 22, line 5, that you returned to Visegrad in July. Is that correct, that you returned in July to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: When I what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you left Novi Pazar and returned to Visegrad, did you do that in July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: June. June. Same month.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Novi Pazar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Single night. Single night. That's how long I was there for, and she stayed with her, and then at about 11 there was a bus out of town, and that was the bus I took on my way back, and I said I'd go back again, but I didn't because we agreed that I should have a go at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to intervene. The question Mr. Groome just asked actually misstated the transcript. The reference does not say he returned to Visegrad in July. So again, if Mr. Groome is going to hold me to a standard of citing to the record, allow him to cite to the record. It says: "So later when we fled the area altogether, they all assembled and formed this group" -- "somewhat larger group. I think it was July at this time already..." So clearly Mr. Groome's question does not state the evidence accurately as it appears on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome. Pay more attention to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm happy to be held to a similarly high standard, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can you explain to us why, after being arrested twice in Visegrad, having the police come and threaten to take you again to the police station, of seeking Mr. Lukic's assistance to escape Visegrad, why it is that you returned so quickly to the town of Visegrad and returned in the way that you did, not by entering through Bosnian-held territory but going straight through the middle into where the very people that had detained you before were likely to catch you again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I think I explained that to you already. It's not a problem. I went back once I put up my girlfriend there. That was when I felt safe, and then I went back because going into Visegrad was no problem at all, and I went back because my brother and my father were still there, and no one at the time was aware of my whereabouts or what I was doing. Okay. That much is obvious, so I went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, in your mind Milan Lukic saved your life, is that not correct, and the life of your fiancee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: In my opinion, yes, he did. He saved me. But I don't know how things would have proceeded from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, his indictment has been public for many years now. Why did you not come forward of your own accord and tell the Office of the Prosecutor or local police or any governmental authority in your own country that you had information that could exonerate an innocent man of extremely serious charges? Why did you not come forward of your own volition with this information earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I think that I replied to that because to this day I would not ask for the measures if I could -- I mean, I really couldn't say anything of my own initiative and even this, that I'm here. Do you understand what I'm saying? That's why I asked for these protective measures because where I live, there, as I said, the people don't like him. There are these stories, there's television, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, sir, I happen to know your father and your cousin quite well, and I believe they would say that I'm a trustworthy individual. Did you never discuss with your father or your cousin the possibility of bringing this information to the attention of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would object to Mr. Groome testifying as to what other people, out-of-court declarants would say about him. I think it's an improper question in that regard. If he rephrased it, maybe it can be presented in a way that it's not objectionable, but I believe as stated it is objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Reformulate it, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, close members of your family have had significant and repeated contacts with the Office of the Prosecutor here in The Hague. Did it never occur to you that this very important information which could exonerate the man who saved your life, did it never occur to you that you could bring this information to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: It's like this: To this day, no one other than my father knows that I'm here. I'm not about to go and talk about it, if you understand what I'm saying. I didn't tell anyone, if you understand me, what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, your father was a protected witness in this Tribunal. Has his identity ever been compromised in the seven years since he testified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: I didn't hear of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Last question, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I hope to finish within the time-period that we have. We still have -- well, can we call up 1D220061, and that should be linked with 1D220059, but not broadcast to the public. This ought to be the original Bosnian statement of this witness along with the official CLSS translation of the same, and if we can turn to page 2 of the B/C/S version, Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to clarify, the ambiguity as to translation that Mr. Groome introduced, if you look, sir, at the centre of this page that you have in front of you, of your statement, do you see there what it says? Does it say -- does it say -- in the Bosnian language, is it four days or four nights that you stayed in the Belgrade apartment there in the middle of the page where it says "tusmo"? Is it four days or four nights in the Bosnian original that you signed, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD1
utterances.text: Four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Your Honours, for giving the full and complete and accurate statement in the official language of the Tribunal, we would tender this version with the official CLSS translation, and then I can -- as the next available 1D exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D101 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I believe for the last -- for the last questions, just to be the on the safe side, I should go into private session as it relates to issues that might identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Sir, we are in open session, and I have no further questions for you. I just want to thank you again on behalf of the Defence of Milan Lukic for making the difficult decision to come here as a Bosnian Muslim to testify on behalf of the Defence. I thank you very much. I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it, and you may now leave. At this stage, I think we will adjourn and hear the next witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before we leave, we have not received any exhibits for the next witness. Am I to take from that that there will be no exhibits used with this next witness, it being less than 48 hours at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a fair assumption?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's a fair assumption, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 23rd day of January, 2009, at 8.50 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.42 p.m.,
